territory: Authentication core and account lifecycle (src/lib/auth.ts, auth-tokens.ts, email-verification.ts, human-pass*, turnstile.ts, login-attempt.ts, member-gate.ts, app-secret.ts, timing-safe.ts, password-rule.ts, origin-rule.ts, verification-mail.ts, next-path.ts, api/auth + api/dev-login, components/auth/* actions, onboarding server side, roster*, normalize.ts, batch-line/utils, plus load-bearing adjacents: email-queue.ts, email.ts, rate-limit.ts, settings/actions.ts, proxy.ts, account-purge.ts, retention.ts, schema User/AuthToken/LoginAttempt/Group models)

findings.title: Email is stored and looked up with raw case at signup/login while the reset flow lowercases: mixed-case signups get false 'Invalid email or password' at login, can NEVER receive a password-reset mail, and one mailbox can register twice
findings.expected: One canonical form of an email address across signup, login, reset and duplicate-detection, so foo@x.com, Foo@x.com and 'Foo@x.com ' are the same account everywhere (orchestrator seed S-A1).
findings.actual: Signup stores the address exactly as typed (signupSchema: `email: z.email("Please enter a valid email")` — zod v4 z.email() validates format only, no trim/lowercase; the create writes `email: parsed.data.email` verbatim; User.email is a plain case-sensitive `String @unique`). Login looks up the RAW submitted string: authorize() does `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } })` while only the rate-limit key is normalized (`const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase()`). The reset flow normalizes the OTHER way: requestPasswordReset does `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase()` then `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })`. Three concrete member-facing failures follow. (1) A member who signed up as Foo@x.com and later types foo@x.com (or vice versa — phone autofill and contact cards routinely change case) gets 'Invalid email or password' forever, because the Postgres lookup is case-sensitive. (2) Any member whose stored email contains an uppercase letter can NEVER receive a reset mail: the lowercased lookup misses their row, `if (!user?.password) return { ok: true }` answers the standard success screen, and nothing ever arrives — a silent, permanent lockout with no error anywhere (the anti-oracle design makes the failure invisible by construction). (3) Duplicate registration: registerUser's existing-account check (`findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } })`) and the DB unique constraint are both case-sensitive, so Foo@x.com registers cleanly beside an existing foo@x.com — two accounts, one mailbox, both confirmable (verify links go to the same inbox). Secondary inconsistencies confirm the drift: LoginAttempt rows are lowercased (`input.email.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 200)`), roster matching lowercases (`where: { email: user.email.toLowerCase() }`), the human-pass HMAC lowercases (`email.toLowerCase()` in signHumanPass) — the auth lookups are the only case-sensitive ones left. The login input is a controlled component storing `e.target.value` raw; no client normalizes.
findings.evidence: src/lib/auth.ts:62 `const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase();` vs src/lib/auth.ts:102-104 `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email }, });` — the same function normalizes for rate limiting but not for the account lookup. src/components/auth/email-actions.ts:160-166 `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase(); ... const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw }, ...})` — reset lookup is lowercase-only, so a stored 'Foo@x.com' can never match. src/components/auth/actions.ts:103-105 `const existing = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } });` and :149 `email: parsed.data.email,` — signup stores and dedupes raw. src/lib/validators.ts:18 `email: z.email("Please enter a valid email"),` — no transform, no max length. prisma/schema.prisma:13 `email String @unique` — case-sensitive text unique. src/lib/login-attempt.ts:49 `email: input.email.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 200)` — proves the codebase's own canonical form is trim+lowercase everywhere except the two auth lookups.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only SQL against the shared DB proves whether members are ALREADY affected: SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email); any nonzero count is a member who today cannot reset their password. A full live proof (register Foo@…, sign out, sign in as foo@…) writes a row, so use a throwaway test address and delete via the admin surface afterwards, or accept the code argument.
findings.fixDirection: Pick trim().toLowerCase() as the canonical form (the codebase already uses it in four places). Apply it (a) in signupSchema via z.email().trim().toLowerCase() or in registerUser before the existing-check and create; (b) in authorize() — look up by acctKey, which already exists; (c) leave requestPasswordReset as is; (d) add a max length (e.g. .max(200)) to the signup email to match displayEmail's cap. Then backfill: UPDATE "User" SET email = lower(email) WHERE email <> lower(email) — but FIRST check for case-variant duplicate pairs (SELECT lower(email) FROM "User" GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1) and merge those by hand before the update, or the unique constraint aborts the backfill. Also mirror the normalization in dev-login's lookup for tooling consistency.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test in the -rule style: a signup/login/reset round-trip helper asserting all three paths resolve 'FoO@x.com ' to the same row; plus a security-regressions-style static check that no prisma.user lookup uses an unnormalized email. A Playwright spec pinning signup-then-relogin with changed case.

findings.title: Onboarding photo step posts the raw picked file (up to 15MB) through a server action; Vercel's ~4.5MB platform body cap kills typical phone photos with an opaque error at the first-run moment
findings.expected: A new member picking a normal phone photo (5–12MB is typical for modern phones) during the onboarding wizard has it uploaded, or is downscaled/cropped client-side first so the bytes on the wire fit — exactly what the profile page's avatar path and the feed's /api/upload path already do.
findings.actual: PhotoStep validates only `if (file.size > 15 * 1024 * 1024)` and then ships the original bytes straight into the updateAvatar server action: `const fd = new FormData(); fd.set("file", file); const result = await updateAvatar(fd);`. There is no crop dialog and no downscaleImage call on this path (AttachImageDialog explicitly has 'no opinion about size/format limits'). On Vercel, request bodies above ~4.5MB are rejected by the PLATFORM (413 FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE) before the function runs — the `serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "25mb" }` in next.config.ts only lifts Next's own guard and cannot raise Vercel's cap. So any photo between ~4.5MB and 15MB passes every client check, then dies at the edge; the action never executes, the client's `result.error` handling never gets a structured error, and the member sees a generic failure on the very first flow they touch. The project has already diagnosed this exact hazard twice elsewhere: image-downscale.ts's header comment ('a route handler's request body is hard-capped at about 4.5MB... a normal phone photo (often 5 to 12MB) sailed past the client check and then died at Vercel's edge with an opaque failure') and letterhead-profile.tsx ('a 6MB phone photo could die on Vercel's ~4.5MB serverless body cap'), whose avatar path was fixed with a client-side crop that produces a small webp blob. The onboarding step reuses the same server action but never received the same client-side fix.
findings.evidence: src/components/onboarding/steps/photo-step.tsx:42-49 `if (file.size > 15 * 1024 * 1024) { toast.error("Photo must be under 15MB"); return; } setBusy(true); const fd = new FormData(); fd.set("file", file); const result = await updateAvatar(fd);` — raw file, no downscale, no crop. src/components/settings/actions.ts:20 `const MAX_AVATAR_INPUT = 15 * 1024 * 1024; // 15MB input` — the server-side cap promises 15MB but can never see more than ~4.5MB on Vercel. next.config.ts:111-112 `serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "25mb" }` — configures Next, not the platform. src/components/profile/letterhead-profile.tsx:363-365 comment: 'the old path shipped the ORIGINAL bytes... a 6MB phone photo could die on Vercel's ~4.5MB serverless body cap' — the same team's own statement of the failure mode this step still has.
findings.reproPlan: Local dev won't reproduce (no platform cap); code-argument-only, or a one-off probe on a preview/prod deployment with a throwaway account and a 6MB JPEG at the onboarding photo step, observing the 413 in the network tab.
findings.fixDirection: Run the picked file through the existing downscaleImage() (2048px webp, already in src/lib/image-downscale.ts) before fd.set in PhotoStep — one import and one line — or route the step through the same crop dialog letterhead-profile uses. Optionally also lower MAX_AVATAR_INPUT/client caps to something the platform can actually carry (~4MB) so the error copy stops promising 15MB.
findings.gateOrTest: A unit test asserting PhotoStep's pick handler produces a payload under 4MB for an oversized input (jsdom + a stubbed downscale), or at minimum a grep-style regression test that every `fd.set("file", ...)` call site references downscaleImage or a crop dialog.

findings.title: Auth is fail-closed on every Cloudflare failure except the narrowest one: a missing Turnstile token is always refused, so a blocked/failed widget script (or a Cloudflare outage, or siteverify answering 200 {success:false,'internal-error'}) locks members out of sign-in, signup and reset — and the widget's own comment believes the opposite
findings.expected: The stated posture (turnstile.ts header: 'a bot check that takes sign-in down with it whenever a third party blinks would be a worse bug than the bots') — a Cloudflare failure degrades to open, and the two files agree on what happens when the widget cannot produce a token.
findings.actual: The fail-open branch only covers the case where a token EXISTS but the siteverify fetch throws/times out (turnstile.ts:102-105). Two other Cloudflare failure modes fail closed. (1) No token: turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;`. The widget produces null whenever the challenge script cannot load or errors (`s.onerror`/`error-callback` set dead=true; getToken 12s timeout resolves null) — which is what happens under an ad/privacy blocker, a corporate proxy that blocks challenges.cloudflare.com, or a Cloudflare outage (the widget network being down is the COMMON outage shape; siteverify-reachable-but-widget-down and vice versa rarely split). The login/signup/forgot clients then submit without a token and authorize()/verifyHumanFromForm refuse with the bot-check error. For a member whose network blocks the script this is permanent: they can never sign in, sign up, or request a reset, and the human-pass cookie cannot help (it is only minted by signup/reset, which are themselves behind the same wall). (2) siteverify reachable but degraded: Cloudflare returns HTTP 200 with `{"success": false, "error-codes": ["internal-error"]}` during partial outages (their docs say to retry it); turnstile.ts:100-101 `const data = (await res.json())...; return data.success === true;` treats that as a forged token and refuses. The contradiction is documented in the code itself: turnstile-widget.tsx:18-21 claims 'the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture... matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in', while turnstile.ts:19 says 'A request with NO token is refused in both environments alike.' One of the two beliefs is wrong, and the shipped behavior is the fail-closed one.
findings.evidence: src/lib/turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;` (unconditional). src/lib/turnstile.ts:100-101 `const data = (await res.json()) as { success?: boolean }; return data.success === true;` — no res.ok check, no error-codes handling, so 'internal-error' (Cloudflare's own transient-failure signal, delivered as HTTP 200) reads as a bot. src/components/auth/turnstile-widget.tsx:18-21 comment: 'If the script cannot load or the challenge errors, getToken() settles to null and the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture (refuse a bad token, fail open only when Cloudflare itself is down) matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in.' — the server does not match. src/components/auth/turnstile-widget.tsx:107-110 `"error-callback": () => { dead.current = true; waiters.current.splice(0).forEach((w) => w(null)); }` — every widget failure funnels to a null token.
findings.reproPlan: Locally: block challenges.cloudflare.com in DevTools network conditions on a TURNSTILE_DEV_REAL=1 dev server (or read-only argue from code, since dev pins the always-pass test key); the widget errors, getToken resolves null, and sign-in answers the bot-check refusal. No production write needed.
findings.fixDirection: Decide the posture deliberately and make the files agree. If availability wins (the stated intent): treat a missing token as fail-open WHEN the account-level protections still stand (rate limits still count, password still checked) — e.g. accept token-less requests but consume rate-limit budget, or retry/pass on siteverify 'internal-error' codes. If security wins: fix the widget comment, and give the member an actionable error ('our human-check service could not load; disable content blockers or try later') instead of the generic bot-check sentence. At minimum, handle the documented 'internal-error' code as retry/fail-open in verifyTurnstile.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on verifyTurnstile with a mocked fetch returning 200 {success:false,'error-codes':['internal-error']} pinning the chosen posture; a second test for the null-token path documenting the decision.

findings.title: recordLoginAttempt (and the AuthToken expiry sweep) are fire-and-forget prisma writes with no after()/waitUntil, so on Vercel the insert races the lambda freeze and the sign-in analytics the owner will lean on at launch are silently lossy
findings.expected: Work that must survive the response on serverless is wrapped in after()/waitUntil (the codebase already knows this: requestPasswordReset's enqueue was moved into after() as audit L3, and the consume() calls in authorize are explicitly 'Awaited so a serverless instance cannot freeze before the count lands').
findings.actual: recordLoginAttempt fires `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...}).catch(...)` and returns void by design ('Deliberately not awaited... A statistics row must never be able to delay, or fail, a sign-in'). On Vercel, once authorize() returns/throws and NextAuth sends the response, the instance freezes; an in-flight insert may complete only if the instance thaws for a later request, or never if it is reaped. The rate-limited and bot-check branches are worst: `recordLoginAttempt({ email, ok: false, reason: "rate-limited" }); throw new RateLimitedLogin();` — the throw ends the request in the same tick the insert starts. These rows are the entire data source for the admin analytics 'who cannot sign in' panel, which the code's own comments call 'the one place the owner would ever notice somebody locked out who should not be' — under launch load that panel will silently undercount by whatever fraction of inserts lose the race, which is undetectable from inside the product. Same class, same file family: mintToken's opportunistic sweep `void prisma.authToken.deleteMany({ where: { expiresAt: { lt: ... } } }).catch(...)` — minting runs inside the mail drain's after() callback, which awaits drainMailQueue but not this orphan promise, so the sweep's completion also races the freeze; since it is the ONLY cleanup for AuthToken ('a project that has no cron' — note retention.ts sweeps LoginAttempt/AuditLog/OutboundEmail but NOT AuthToken), dead token rows will mostly accumulate in production (small rows, slow growth — a hygiene failure rather than a scale one at 2,000 users).
findings.evidence: src/lib/login-attempt.ts:46-54 `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({ data: {...} }).catch((err) => {...})` — no await, no after(). src/lib/auth.ts:72-74 `if (!ipOk || !acctOk) { recordLoginAttempt({ email, ok: false, reason: "rate-limited" }); throw new RateLimitedLogin(); }` — insert launched and abandoned in the same statement as the throw. Contrast src/lib/auth.ts:96-98 'Awaited so a serverless instance cannot freeze before the count lands' — the adjacent rate-limit spend acknowledges the exact failure mode this write is exposed to. src/lib/auth-tokens.ts:107-118 `void prisma.authToken.deleteMany({ where: { expiresAt: { lt: new Date(Date.now() - 7 * 24 * 60 * 60_000) } } }).catch(...)` — same fire-and-forget; src/lib/retention.ts KEEP_DAYS covers loginAttempts/auditLogs/outboundEmails but has no AuthToken step.
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only (freeze behavior is a platform property; local dev keeps the process alive and will always show the row landing). A production-side read-only check after launch week: compare LoginAttempt counts against Vercel request logs for /api/auth/callback/credentials.
findings.fixDirection: In recordLoginAttempt, attempt `after(() => prisma.loginAttempt.create(...))` (authorize runs inside the NextAuth route handler's request scope, so after() is available; keep the current void-promise as the fallback for non-request contexts, mirroring scheduleDrain's try/catch pattern in email-queue.ts:364-377). Alternatively await the insert behind a short timeout — a single ~10ms insert cannot meaningfully delay sign-in and the .catch already protects the return value. For the AuthToken sweep: either await it inside mintToken (it already runs post-response inside the drain's after()), or add an authToken step to runRetentionSweep, which is the project's real home for table hygiene.
findings.gateOrTest: The security-regressions/gate-coverage test family: a static check that `void prisma.` never appears outside an after() wrapper, or a unit test on recordLoginAttempt asserting it registers with after() when a request scope exists.

findings.title: joinBatchGroup is find-then-create with no unique constraint on Group.name: two same-batch alumni signing up concurrently create two 'Batch of {year}' groups, silently splitting the batch for group-scoped posts and Catch-ups
findings.expected: Exactly one 'Batch of {year}' group per batch, however many members of that batch register simultaneously — per the taxonomy, an 'only one per X' rule is real only if a DB unique constraint enforces it (6c/6d check-then-insert TOCTOU).
findings.actual: registerUser → joinBatchGroup does `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({...}) }`. Group.name is `name String` with no @@unique, so two concurrent registrations from one batch (the launch-day scenario the mail queue was explicitly built for: 'more than 100 signups on the first day') can both read 'no group' and both create one — permanently duplicating the batch container with nothing to stop it and nothing to detect it. The code's own comment concedes the gap ('Group.name is not unique in the schema, so match by exact name'). Groups are retired as UI but remain load-bearing: group membership gates post visibility (feed actions read `prisma.groupMember.findMany({ where: { userId } })` and filter posts by `OR: [{ groupId: null }, { groupId: { in: groupIds } }]`) and Catch-ups hang off Group rows (Catchup has a 1:1 `catchup Catchup?` relation on Group). With a split batch, members auto-joined to duplicate A cannot see group posts or batch Catch-ups attached to duplicate B, and later members from the same batch land in whichever duplicate findFirst returns first (no orderBy, so it is not even deterministic which one accretes members). There is no admin surface for merging groups, so the split is permanent without SQL.
findings.evidence: src/components/auth/actions.ts:215-230 `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name }, select: { id: true } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({ data: { name, ... } }) }` — classic read-then-create race. prisma/schema.prisma:191-208 Group model: `name String` with only `@@index([visibility, createdAt])`, no unique on name. src/app/(main)/feed/actions.ts:955-972 membership-derived `groupIds` gating `OR: [{ groupId: null }, { groupId: { in: groupIds } }]` — the concrete surface where a member in the wrong duplicate loses visibility.
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only for the race itself (a live proof needs two concurrent real signups against the shared production DB). A read-only check for whether it has ALREADY happened: SELECT name, count(*) FROM "Group" WHERE name LIKE 'Batch of %' GROUP BY name HAVING count(*) > 1.
findings.fixDirection: Add a unique constraint that pins the invariant — either `@@unique([name])` (batch groups are the only auto-created names; verify no legit duplicate names exist first with the read above) or a dedicated nullable `batchYear Int? @unique` column on Group for batch containers — then replace findFirst/create with a single upsert on that key, and keep a P2002 catch that re-reads the winner. The GroupMember upsert half is already race-safe.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on joinBatchGroup simulating the race (two calls with the create mocked to interleave, asserting one group id), plus the schema constraint itself, which makes the DB the test.

findings.title: Legacy /onboarding page's updateProfile server action writes seven profile columns with zero validation — no length caps, no schema, no normalization — bypassing every rule profileSchema enforces on the same columns
findings.expected: Every write path to a profile column enforces the same rules (the codebase's own standard: contactMethodsSchema exists precisely because 'this is the second write path to them, so it gets the same gate' — audit M18 closed exactly this class on updateContactMethods).
findings.actual: src/app/(auth)/onboarding/actions.ts exports updateProfile, which takes FormData and writes `bio, currentCity, workplace, jobTitle, phone, instagram, linkedin` with only `if (value && value.trim()) data[field] = value.trim()` — no Zod, no length limits, no normalizePhone, no titleCase. The live /onboarding page (still routed, still imports and calls it) enforces `maxLength={1000}` only in the client textarea; a direct POST to the action (every 'use server' export is a public HTTP endpoint) stores arbitrarily large strings — a multi-megabyte bio (bounded only by the 25mb bodySizeLimit locally / 4.5MB on Vercel) lands in User.bio and is then fetched and rendered on every surface that selects bio, degrading profile and directory reads for everyone who views that member. It also skips the normalization contract: a phone stored here is un-normalized ('(080) 4123 5678' instead of digits), workplace/city skip titleCase, so the directory's assumption that 'every stored number reads the same way' quietly breaks. The 2026-08-20 mass-assignment hardening covered src/components/settings/actions.ts but this parallel legacy action was missed; the gate-coverage test passes it because it does contain `await auth()` — the sweep proves shape, not validation, exactly as its own comment warns.
findings.evidence: src/app/(auth)/onboarding/actions.ts:12-27 `const data: Record<string, string | null> = {}; const fields = ["bio", "currentCity", "workplace", "jobTitle", "phone", "instagram", "linkedin"]; for (const field of fields) { const value = formData.get(field) as string | null; if (value && value.trim()) { data[field] = value.trim(); } } if (Object.keys(data).length > 0) { await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: session.user.id }, data }); }` — the entire action; no schema import anywhere in the file. Contrast src/lib/validators.ts:53-67 profileSchema capping the same columns (`bio: z.string().max(1000)`, `currentCity: z.string().max(100)`, `phone: z.string().max(24)`, etc.). src/app/(auth)/onboarding/page.tsx:16,26 shows the action is live (`import { updateProfile } from "./actions"; ... await updateProfile(formData);`).
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only, or on local dev (shared DB — use your own test account): POST the action with a 100KB bio via the /onboarding form with the client maxLength removed in DevTools; confirm the column stores it. Clean up by re-saving a normal bio.
findings.fixDirection: Either delete the legacy /onboarding route + action outright (the /welcome wizard with saveOnboardingRegister supersedes it — confirm nothing else links to /onboarding, note proxy.ts DEMO_CLOSED_PATHS lists it) or validate through profileSchema (or a pick() of it) and run phone through normalizePhone / free-text through titleCase like every sibling action does. Deleting is the better move: one fewer write path to keep in sync.
findings.gateOrTest: If kept: extend gate-coverage-style static checks so every action writing User profile columns references a validator schema. If deleted: the lab-registry/route audit in npm run check plus a security-regressions test pinning the file gone.

findings.title: A database error during sign-in surfaces as 'Invalid email or password.', sending members with correct passwords into a doomed reset loop during any DB blip
findings.expected: 6k: DB slow/down mid-request — the member sees something actionable ('something went wrong on our side, try again in a minute'), not an accusation that their credentials are wrong.
findings.actual: When any awaited call in authorize() throws for infrastructure reasons (the findUnique, bcrypt on a malformed row, the deletion-cancel update), the error is not a CredentialsSignin subclass, so NextAuth surfaces a generic error result with no recognised code. The login client maps every unrecognised code to the credentials sentence: `setError(code === "rate-limited" ? RATE_LIMITED : code === "bot-check" ? BOT_CHECK_FAILED : "Invalid email or password.")`. During a Supabase hiccup every member signing in is told their password is wrong; the natural next step (forgot-password) also fails or silently no-ops against the same down DB, compounding confusion at exactly the moment support load spikes. The client's try/catch 'Something went wrong' branch never fires because signIn({redirect:false}) resolves with an error field rather than throwing.
findings.evidence: src/app/(auth)/login/login-client.tsx:385-397 `const code = (result as { code?: string | null }).code; setError(code === "rate-limited" ? RATE_LIMITED : code === "bot-check" ? BOT_CHECK_FAILED : "Invalid email or password.");` — the fall-through claims a credential failure for every unrecognised error, including NextAuth's Configuration/CallbackRouteError shapes produced by an authorize() throw. src/lib/auth.ts:15-26 documents that only CredentialsSignin subclasses carry clean codes, i.e. every other throw arrives here code-less.
findings.reproPlan: Local dev: point DATABASE_URL at an unreachable host (or drop network mid-request via chrome-devtools), submit the login form, observe 'Invalid email or password.' — read-only, no shared-DB writes.
findings.fixDirection: In the login client, distinguish NextAuth's non-credentials error strings (result.error === "Configuration" / "CallbackRouteError", or simply: code undefined AND result.error not "CredentialsSignin") and show the transient-failure sentence instead. Optionally catch unexpected throws inside authorize() and rethrow a dedicated CredentialsSignin subclass with code "server-error" so the channel carries it cleanly like rate-limited/bot-check already do.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on the error-mapping helper (extract the ternary into a testable function) covering codes: rate-limited, bot-check, undefined-with-CredentialsSignin, undefined-with-Configuration.

findings.title: The deletion-scheduled email renders the purge date in server UTC (toLocaleDateString with no timeZone), so IST members deleting between 05:30–24:00 IST are told a purge day one day earlier than their local day-of-purge
findings.expected: Dates shown to members reflect their timezone (members are in IST, +5:30; servers run UTC) — the codebase knows this rule elsewhere: nextBudgetResetAt() is 'returned as a Date and formatted in the BROWSER's timezone by whoever shows it'.
findings.actual: requestAccountDeletion computes `purgeAt = new Date(Date.now() + DELETION_GRACE_DAYS * 86_400_000)` and formats it SERVER-side into the email: `purgeAt.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "long", year: "numeric" })` — no timeZone option, so on Vercel this renders the UTC calendar day. A member confirming deletion any time from 05:30 IST onward has a purgeAt whose IST date is one day later than its UTC date; the mail (their only written record, and 'the takeover alarm') names a day that, in their timezone, is the day BEFORE the purge moment. Off-by-one in the safe direction (they believe they have less time, not more), but it is a wrong date in the one message that exists to state a deadline, and the audit-log detail (`purgeAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10)`) records the same UTC day, so the two 'receipts' agree with each other and disagree with the member's calendar.
findings.evidence: src/components/settings/actions.ts:315 `const purgeAt = new Date(Date.now() + DELETION_GRACE_DAYS * 86_400_000);` and :344-348 `purgeDate: purgeAt.toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "long", year: "numeric" }),` — no timeZone, evaluated in the server's zone (UTC on Vercel). Compare src/lib/email-queue.ts:517-519 which deliberately defers formatting to the browser for exactly this reason.
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only (deterministic from the Intl call; a live proof would schedule a real account's deletion).
findings.fixDirection: Pass `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` to the toLocaleDateString call (the membership is IST by charter), or format with an explicit zone in the email template layer alongside a time-of-day, matching the 'a real clock time is a promise somebody can check' principle.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on the purge-date formatting with a fixed timestamp of 20:00 UTC asserting the IST day is rendered.

findings.title: requestVerification ignores the conditional updateMany count, so two simultaneous requests both notify the admins; and the delete-then-recreate place writers can duplicate rows under two-tab saves
findings.expected: The conditional write is the dedupe: whoever loses the updateMany race skips the side effect (the pattern tryRosterAutoVerify itself uses correctly at roster.ts:77-85); wholesale list replacement is atomic against a concurrent replacement of the same list.
findings.actual: Two independent small races. (1) requestVerification: `const already = session.user.verifyState === "pending"; if (!already) { await prisma.user.updateMany({ where: { id: ..., verifyState: "unverified" }, data: { verifyState: "pending" } }); await notifyAdmins(...); }` — two concurrent invocations (double-click before the dialog's pending state lands, or two tabs) both read verifyState 'unverified' from their request-cached sessions, both run updateMany (one matches, one matches zero rows), and BOTH call notifyAdmins because the count is never checked → duplicate admin notifications for one person. (2) saveOnboardingRegister and updateUserPlaces both replace UserPlace rows via deleteMany-then-createMany inside a transaction; UserPlace has no unique on (userId, position), so two overlapping saves at READ COMMITTED can interleave as T1-delete, T2-delete(sees 0 after T1 commits or concurrently), T1-create, T2-create → the member's city list holds both sets, showing duplicate city chips on the profile and doubled pins on the map until the next save wholesale-replaces them. Both are self-limiting (a repeat click / a re-save heals them) — hence Low — but both are the exact 6c lost-update/double-submit shape with one-line guards available.
findings.evidence: src/components/auth/verification-actions.ts:51-62 `const already = session.user.verifyState === "pending"; if (!already) { await prisma.user.updateMany({ where: { id: session.user.id, verifyState: "unverified" }, ... }); await notifyAdmins(...) }` — updateMany's count discarded; notifyAdmins unconditional inside the branch. src/components/onboarding/actions.ts:92-105 `await tx.userPlace.deleteMany({ where: { userId } }); if (cleanedPlaces.length > 0) { await tx.userPlace.createMany({...}) }` and src/components/settings/actions.ts:162-181 same delete/create pattern; prisma/schema.prisma:659-677 UserPlace has `@@index([userId])` but no unique constraint that a doubled insert would violate.
findings.reproPlan: Local dev with own test account (shared DB — self-healing writes only): fire requestVerification twice in parallel from the console and observe two admin notifications; fire updateUserPlaces twice in parallel with different lists and read the doubled UserPlace rows, then re-save once to heal.
findings.fixDirection: (1) Use the updateMany result: `const changed = await prisma.user.updateMany(...); if (changed.count > 0) await notifyAdmins(...)` — the row transition becomes the dedupe, exactly like the roster verify. (2) Add `@@unique([userId, position])` to UserPlace (makes the doubled createMany fail loudly instead of silently duplicating) and/or take a per-user advisory-free guard such as deleteMany-with-createMany keyed on a version column; at minimum disable the save buttons while pending.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting notifyAdmins is skipped when updateMany reports 0; schema constraint on UserPlace doubles as the test for (2).

findings.title: Signup derives batchType from an unvalidated (yearLeft, batchYear) pair: batchTypeFromLeaving happily returns 'ISC' for impossible inputs (batchYear earlier than yearLeft), unlike its sibling computeBatchFromSchooling which rejects them
findings.expected: The same sanity window the derive-from-schooling path enforces ('Those years add up to past 12th grade' when gradeAtLeaving > 12): a member's batchYear cannot be before their yearLeft, and a typo produces an error, not a silently wrong board credential.
findings.actual: signupSchema validates each year only against absolute bounds (1926..now+1 / now+7) and the action checks only `yearLeft < yearJoined`; nothing relates batchYear to yearLeft. registerUser then calls `batchType = batchTypeFromLeaving(parsed.data.yearLeft!, batchYear)` where `const gradeAtLeaving = 12 - (batchYear - yearLeft)` — a member who fat-fingers batchYear 2015 with yearLeft 2018 gets gradeAtLeaving 15 → 'ISC' stored; batchYear 2035 with yearLeft 2010 gets a negative grade → null batchType (reads as 'mid-school leaver'). Both are silently wrong facts on the profile and in directory filters, and the same unchecked pair flows through updateUserProfile (settings/actions.ts:86-91) on every later edit. computeBatchFromSchooling proves the intended envelope exists (`if (gradeAtLeaving > 12) return { ok: false, error: "Those years add up to past 12th grade..." }`) — the direct-entry path just never got it.
findings.evidence: src/lib/utils.ts:250-258 `export function batchTypeFromLeaving(yearLeft: number, batchYear: number): "ISC" | "ICSE" | null { const gradeAtLeaving = 12 - (batchYear - yearLeft); if (gradeAtLeaving >= 12) return "ISC"; ... }` — no upper bound on gradeAtLeaving. src/components/auth/actions.ts:90-93 `batchYear = parsed.data.batchYear!; batchType = batchTypeFromLeaving(parsed.data.yearLeft!, batchYear);` with no batchYear>=yearLeft refinement anywhere in src/lib/validators.ts:14-45. Contrast src/lib/utils.ts:322-328 (computeBatchFromSchooling) rejecting gradeAtLeaving > 12.
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only (pure function; a unit assertion demonstrates it: batchTypeFromLeaving(2018, 2015) === 'ISC').
findings.fixDirection: Add a refine to signupSchema (and profileSchema/updateUserProfile's batch block): batchYear >= yearLeft, and optionally batchYear - yearLeft <= 11 (cannot leave more than 11 years before your batch finishes 12th, i.e. gradeAtLeaving >= 1). Or make batchTypeFromLeaving return null (with the caller surfacing an error) when gradeAtLeaving > 12 or < 1, mirroring computeBatchFromSchooling's envelope.
findings.gateOrTest: Extend batch-line.test.mjs / a utils test with the impossible pairs pinning the rejection; schema refine test for signupSchema.

findings.title: confirmEmailToken and resetPassword burn the single-use token before applying its effect, outside any transaction: a crash or DB error in the gap consumes the member's link with nothing to show for it
findings.expected: 6d: the token consume and the write it authorizes either both land or neither (or the consume happens last), so a transient failure never leaves a member holding a dead link that did nothing.
findings.actual: confirmEmailToken: `const read = await readToken(token, "verify", { consume: true });` marks the AuthToken used, THEN `await prisma.user.update({ ..., data: { emailVerified: new Date() } })` — a serverless timeout, DB blip or crash between the two leaves the token spent and the email unconfirmed; the member's next click says 'already confirmed' (the used-token branch returns "already" without verifying the address actually is confirmed — the comment claims 'if the address really is confirmed, say so plainly' but the code never checks) while the gate still blocks them, a genuinely confusing contradiction. resetPassword has the same shape: consume at :252, bcrypt.hash (~100ms window) and the user.update at :266 after it — a failure in between burns the reset link with the password unchanged. Both have recovery paths (resend, re-request) so this is Low, but the recovery is rate-limited (verify 5/hour, reset 4/30min) and the 'already' lie in confirmEmailToken turns a transient blip into a support ticket.
findings.evidence: src/components/auth/email-actions.ts:104-121: `const read = await readToken(token, "verify", { consume: true }); if (!read.ok) { if (read.reason === "used") { return "already"; } ... } await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: read.userId }, data: { emailVerified: new Date() } });` — consume and effect are two separate awaits with no transaction; the "already" branch never verifies emailVerified is actually set. src/components/auth/email-actions.ts:252-282: consume (`readToken(..., { consume: true })`), then `const hashed = await bcrypt.hash(input.password, 12); await prisma.user.update({...})`. src/lib/auth-tokens.ts:183-191 shows the consume is its own updateMany.
findings.reproPlan: Code-argument-only (needs a fault injected between two awaits).
findings.fixDirection: For confirmEmailToken: perform the consume and the emailVerified update in one prisma.$transaction (both are simple updates — batch form works through pgbouncer), and make the "used" branch honest by checking the row's user.emailVerified before claiming "already" (readToken already selects the user relation; add emailVerified to that select). For resetPassword: hash BEFORE consuming (moves the long await out of the gap), then transaction the consume + user.update together; burnTokens can stay after.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on the "already" outcome asserting it reflects the row's emailVerified state; integration test with a mocked failing user.update asserting the token remains redeemable.
